title: Kings, Seek Wisdom
sum: The speaker turns back to the rulers of the earth he addressed in 1:1. Their power was lent to them by the Lord, who will examine how they used it; the more power they had, the stricter their test will be, for God made small and great alike. So they should learn wisdom.

Then Wisdom herself comes into view: she shines and never fades, she is easily found, she even goes looking for those worthy of her and waits at their gates. A chain of steps leads from longing for discipline to love, to keeping her laws, to incorruption, to nearness to God, to a kingdom. The chapter ends with a promise: the speaker will tell, openly and without envy, what Wisdom is and how she came to be.
readings: Read as advice to rulers

The chapter belongs to a well-known kind of Greek writing, the address to kings on how to rule. It tells them their power is God's gift and that God will hold them to account. Read this way it agrees with Romans 13:1 and with the prophets' words to kings.
Read as an invitation to everyone

The 'kings' may be a literary frame. The real readers were ordinary Jews in a Greek city, and the promise of 6:20–21, a kingdom through wisdom, is the reign of the righteous with God that the book has promised (3:8; 5:16). On this reading every reader is a king in training.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary reads 6:12–16 on the 32nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year A), and 6:1–11 on the Wednesday of the 32nd week (Year I).
views.O: On the book's place in Orthodox Bibles, see the book's front page. The chapter's teaching that a ruler's power is lent by God (6:3) agrees with Romans 13:1 and John 19:11.
views.P: Protestants do not count the book as Scripture, but its teaching on rulers matches Proverbs 8:15–16 and Romans 13:1–4. The chain of 6:17–20 can be compared with Romans 5:3–5.
views.H: Scholars see in the chapter the Greek form of advice to kings and the philosophers' chain argument (sorites). The phrase 'incorruption puts a person close to God' (6:19) draws on Greek ideas of becoming like God, set inside Jewish faith in the God who judges.
views.J: Jewish readers have not used the book in the synagogue, since it is not in the Hebrew Bible, but its teaching that rulers answer to God is shared with the Psalms (Psalm 2:10; 82) and later Jewish teaching on kings.

echoes: Psalm 2:10; Proverbs 8:1–21; Romans 13:1–4; Daniel 2:21; John 19:11; Proverbs 1:20–33; Romans 5:3–5; 1 Corinthians 15:53

settings.by: The book's speaker, whom 7:1–9:18 shows to be Solomon
settings.to: Kings and judges of the earth, as the book addresses them
settings.when: after the judgment scene of chapters 2–5
settings.why: To warn rulers that their power is on loan from God, and to win them to wisdom, which leads to a lasting kingdom. Knowing that the real readers were not kings, the warning becomes comfort: the powerful who oppress the righteous will answer to God, and the humble who love Wisdom will reign.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt (see the book's front page for the place and for the dates proposed, from the reign of Ptolemy IV, 221–204 BC, to AD 41–44), who saw ruler worship around them. For them the call to kings said that every ruler over them answered to their God.
views: Read this way, the book was meant at least in part for Gentile rulers or educated Greeks, to commend Jewish wisdom to them.
Read this way, the address to kings is a convention, and the book was written for Jews, to strengthen them in their faith in a Greek city.

title: A Breath of the Power of God
sum: Now the speaker talks about himself. He is a mortal like everyone, born the same way and bound for the same death. So he prayed, and a spirit of wisdom came to him. He chose her over thrones and gold, and with her came every good thing. She taught him all the sciences of his day: the structure of the world, the elements, the calendar, the stars, animals, plants and the human mind.

The chapter then describes Wisdom herself, with twenty-one marks of her spirit, and with images that became central to Christian thought about the Son: she is a vapor of God's power, an outflow of his glory, a radiance of eternal light, a stainless mirror of his working and an image of his goodness. She is one, yet she can do all things and makes all things new; in every age she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets.
readings: Read as Jewish wisdom in Greek dress

The king of 1 Kings 3 prays and receives wisdom, but the wisdom he receives is described in the language of Greek philosophy: a fine spirit that runs through all things, as the Stoics said, and an outflow of divine light. The writer claims that everything good in Greek learning comes from Israel's God.
Read with the New Testament

Christians have read 7:22–8:1 beside Hebrews 1:3, Colossians 1:15–17 and John 1:1–9. What Wisdom is here, the Son is there: the radiance of God's glory, his image, the one through whom all things were made. Hebrews 1:3 uses the same rare word, apaugasma, 'radiance'.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary reads 7:7–11 on the 28th Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B), 7:22b–8:1 on the Thursday of the 32nd week (Year I), and 7:7–10, 15–16 on the feasts of doctors of the Church such as Thomas Aquinas and Robert Bellarmine. Origen and Athanasius applied the images of 7:25–26 to the Son (see the notes at 7:25–26).
views.O: Origen explained 7:25–26 of the Son (On First Principles 1.2.9), and Athanasius of Alexandria, honored as a father in the Orthodox churches, argued from the radiance image that the Son never was not (Orations against the Arians 1.13).
views.P: Protestants read the chapter as a witness to Jewish thought that shaped the New Testament's language about Christ (Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15), while basing doctrine on the New Testament texts themselves.
views.H: Scholars study the chapter as a meeting of Jewish wisdom and Greek philosophy: a fine spirit that runs through all things (7:22–24) and the language of light and image (7:25–26). Its images stand close to the New Testament's words about Christ (Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15).
views.J: Jewish thinkers of the same city, above all Philo of Alexandria, spoke of God's Wisdom and Word in similar ways. Later rabbinic Judaism identified divine wisdom with the Torah rather than with a heavenly figure.

deep.b: Counting the Greek, the spirit in Wisdom has twenty adjectives and one participle phrase: twenty-one, three times seven. Some describe her mind (intelligent, clear, distinct, sharp), some her purity (holy, unstained, beyond harm, pure), some her power (unstoppable, all-powerful, watching over all), some her goodness (loving the good, doing good, kind to people), and some her movement (quick-moving, fine, making her way through every spirit). The list moves from what she is to what she does, and 7:24–8:1 then explains: she pervades all things because she is pure, and she can do this because she comes from God himself.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the mirror and the image as a teaching order
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not a view I have found stated in this form. The five images of 7:25–26 seem to move from the most material to the most personal: a vapor (something rising from a source), an outflow (something streaming from it), a radiance (light shining from light), a mirror (something that shows another), and an image (something that is like another). Read in that order, the passage teaches a reader step by step that Wisdom is from God, then like God, then the way God is seen. Hebrews 1:3 uses the radiance (apaugasma) and adds a word not in this list, the "exact stamp" (charaktēr); Colossians 1:15 uses the image (eikōn). If those writers knew this passage, which cannot be shown, they took its later steps. The ordering is my reading.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:5–14; 1 Kings 4:29–34; Proverbs 8:22–31; Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15–17; John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 1:24; James 1:5; James 1:17; Revelation 21:5

settings.what: Solomon's speech about how he found Wisdom
settings.by: Solomon, speaking in the first person, though the book never names him
settings.to: The rulers addressed in 6:1–11, and every reader
settings.when: as the king looks back on his life, from his birth to the prayer in which he received wisdom (7:7)
settings.why: To show that even a king is an ordinary mortal, and that his greatness came only from Wisdom, God's gift in answer to prayer. The speech teaches the reader what Wisdom is and how to seek her, and it prepares for the prayer of chapter 9.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt (see the book's front page for the place and for the dates proposed, from the reign of Ptolemy IV, 221–204 BC, to AD 41–44), where the schools taught Plato and the Stoics. For them the list of sciences (7:17–20) and the philosophers' language of 7:22–26 claimed the best of Greek learning for Israel's God.

title: Wisdom as a Bride
sum: Solomon tells how he fell in love with Wisdom when he was young and wanted to bring her home as his bride. She lives with God and knows his secrets; she is richer than wealth, the craftswoman of all things, the teacher of the four great virtues, wise in history, speech and the future. With her he would be honored by elders, feared by rulers, and remembered forever; with her at home there would be no bitterness, only joy.

He thought it over: there is immortality in being joined to her. He had been a gifted child with a good soul, or better, being good he came into an undefiled body. But he knew he could not win her unless God gave her, and knowing that was itself wisdom. So he turned to the Lord in prayer.
readings: Read as a love story

The language is that of courtship and marriage: he loves her, seeks her as a bride, brings her home, rests with her. Solomon, known for his many wives (1 Kings 11:1–4), is pictured as the man whose one true bride was Wisdom.
Read as a philosophy of the soul

Verses 19–20 speak of a good soul and a body it entered, language that sounds like Plato. Whether the writer believed that souls exist before bodies is one of the book's most debated questions (see the card).

views.C: Catholic teaching holds that "every spiritual soul is created immediately by God" and is not produced by the parents (Catechism 366); see the card. The Latin of 8:21, 'I could not be continent unless God gave it,' is the verse Augustine quotes in his Confessions (6.11.20; 10.31.45).
views.O: John of Damascus, the eighth-century father, teaches that body and soul were formed "at one and the same time," against Origen (Exact Exposition 2.12); see the card.
views.P: Protestants do not count the book as Scripture. On where souls come from, Lutheran and Reformed teachers gave different answers: the Lutheran Quenstedt taught that souls are passed on from the parents, while the Reformed Hodge calls creation of each soul by God the common view of the Reformed (see the card). The teaching of 8:21, that wisdom is God's gift, matches James 1:5.
views.H: Scholars note the Greek education behind the chapter: the four virtues of Plato (8:7), the rhetoric of praise, and talk of a good soul and a body (8:19–20). Whether 8:19–20 means that the soul exists before the body is read both ways (see the note at 8:20).
views.J: The Talmud reports Rav Asi's teaching that the Messiah, son of David, "will not come until all the souls of the body have been finished," that is, until every soul destined for a body has entered one (Bavli Yevamot 62a). That implies souls waiting before birth, a view close to one reading of 8:19–20.

echoes: Proverbs 4:6–9; Proverbs 7:4; Proverbs 8:30; Proverbs 31:10–31; 1 Kings 3:7; 1 Kings 10:1; 1 Kings 11:1–4; Song of Songs 4:9; James 1:5

traditions.q: Solomon says, "a good soul was given me as my share. Or better, since I was good, I came into a body without stain" (8:19–20). Does the soul exist before the body, and where does each soul come from? (Whether the soul is immortal by nature or by God's gift is asked on the card at chapter 3.)
views: Each soul is created by God, not passed on from the parents: the Church teaches that "every spiritual soul is created immediately by God - it is not 'produced' by the parents" (Catechism 366).

John of Damascus, an eighth-century father of the church, teaches that "body and soul were formed at one and the same time, not first the one and then the other," as Origen supposed (Exact Exposition 2.12).

The Formula of Concord says that God "at the present day still creates and makes" human nature in people (Solid Declaration I.7), without saying how each soul begins. Johann Andreas Quenstedt (1617–1688), a Lutheran theologian at Wittenberg, teaches that apart from Adam's, human souls are "created, not daily, nor begotten of their parents as the body," but "by virtue of the divine blessing are propagated, per traducem, by their parents" (in Heinrich Schmid's Doctrinal Theology of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, §20).

Charles Hodge, a Presbyterian theologian of the Reformed tradition, teaches that each soul "is not generated or derived from the parents" but "created by the immediate agency of God," calls this the common doctrine "especially of the Reformed theologians," and names Calvin, Beza and Turrettin among them. Of pre-existence he says it "may be said to have begun and ended with Origen" and "does not pretend to be a Scriptural doctrine" (Systematic Theology, vol. 2, part II, ch. 3, §§1, 3).

Yes: human spirits lived with God before their birth on earth. "Man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be" (Doctrine and Covenants 93:29).

deep.h: Origen and the soul before the body
deep.b: Origen of Alexandria (about AD 185–254) taught that God first made all rational beings equal and alike, and that their different states in this world come from the free choices they made before it: "God, who deemed it just to arrange His creatures according to their merit, brought down these different understandings into the harmony of one world" (On First Principles 2.9.6). He supported this from Jacob and Esau, chosen "before they were born" (Romans 9:11; On First Principles 2.9.7). The fifteen anathemas against Origen usually assigned to the Second Council of Constantinople (553) begin by condemning "the fabulous pre-existence of souls." Whether that council adopted them, or a synod at Constantinople in 543, is disputed; Henry Percival's excursus in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers sets out both sides and notes that the council's eleventh canon names Origen among the heretics. John of Damascus later wrote against the idea (Exact Exposition 2.12). Augustine, Hodge notes, was drawn toward traducianism in his debate with Pelagius but "never, however, could bring himself fully to adopt it."

settings.when: as he recalls his youth, before the prayer of chapter 9
settings.why: To make the reader want Wisdom as a lover wants a bride, and to show that even the best natural gifts are not enough: Wisdom must be asked from God. The closing verse (8:21) turns the whole speech into a lesson on prayer.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt (see the book's front page for the place and for the dates proposed, from the reign of Ptolemy IV, 221–204 BC, to AD 41–44). Readers who knew Greek talk of the soul heard their own language in 8:19–20, and the chapter's end (8:21) told them that Wisdom is God's gift, not the prize of a school.

title: Give Me Wisdom
sum: This is Solomon's prayer for wisdom. It recalls the request of 1 Kings 3 and 2 Chronicles 1, but sets it after God's command to build the temple (9:7–8) and names no place. God made all things by his word and formed human beings by his wisdom to rule the world justly. 'Give me Wisdom, who sits beside you on your thrones.' The king is God's slave, weak and short-lived; even a perfect man counts for nothing without God's wisdom. God chose him as king and told him to build a temple, a copy of the holy tent prepared from the beginning. Wisdom was with God at creation: 'Send her' to labor with me.

The last part widens to all humanity. No one can know God's plan; our reasonings are timid, the perishable body weighs the soul down, we hardly understand the earth, let alone heaven. Only if God gives wisdom and sends his Holy Spirit can anyone know his will. That is how those on earth were set on straight paths and saved by Wisdom.
readings: Read as Solomon's prayer

The prayer recalls 1 Kings 3:6–9 and 2 Chronicles 1:8–10: the king's weakness, the great people he must judge, the request for wisdom. But it opens with God's mercy and creation rather than his loyal love to David, it speaks of the command to build the temple, which comes elsewhere (1 Chronicles 28:10–19; 1 Kings 5:5), and it adds what Kings does not have: Wisdom as a person beside God's throne, the heavenly tent, and a meditation on human limits.
Read as everyone's prayer
From 9:13 the 'I' becomes 'we': the prayer speaks for every human being. The Catholic Church reads 9:13–18b on a Sunday, and 9:9–11, 13–18 in the Ritual Mass for the Anointing of the Sick.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary reads 9:13–18b on the 23rd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C), and 9:9–11, 13–18 in the Ritual Mass for the Anointing of the Sick. Augustine quoted 9:15 often (City of God 12.15; 13.16; 14.3), and read it of the body as it now is, after sin.
views.P: For Protestants, who do not count the book as Scripture, 9:13–17 says what 1 Corinthians 2:10–16 says: God's mind is known only by his Spirit. 9:15 can be compared with Paul's hope of resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:1–4); see the note at 9:15.
views.H: Scholars note how the writer retells 1 Kings 3 in the light of Greek philosophy: the body as the soul's burden (Plato, Phaedo 81c), and the heavenly model of the temple, a theme also found in Hebrews 8:5.
views.J: The prayer draws on 1 Kings 3 and on the pattern of the sanctuary shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40), which the temple copies (9:8).

echoes: 1 Kings 3:5–14; 2 Chronicles 1:7–12; 1 Chronicles 28:6–19; 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:17–20; Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5; Isaiah 40:13; Romans 11:33–34; 1 Corinthians 2:10–16; 2 Corinthians 5:1–4; Psalm 116:16

settings.to: God, "God of the fathers, Lord of your mercy"
settings.when: as king, after God has told him to build the sanctuary (9:7–8). The book names no place or time; the request recalls the prayer at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:5–9), and the command to build recalls David's charge (1 Chronicles 28:10)
settings.why: To ask for Wisdom as God's gift, and to teach readers to ask the same. The prayer says that the highest knowledge, of God's will, is given from above (9:13–18).
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt (see the book's front page for the place and for the dates proposed, from the reign of Ptolemy IV, 221–204 BC, to AD 41–44). For them the prayer of Israel's king was a model for their own prayer, and 9:15 spoke of the body in terms their Greek schooling knew.

title: Wisdom Saves the Righteous
sum: Without naming anyone, the chapter retells history from Adam to the Exodus as the story of Wisdom. She guarded the first-formed man and rescued him from his trespass. Cain left her and perished; because of him the earth was flooded, and she steered Noah on a bit of wood. When the nations were confused at Babel, she found Abraham and made him strong at the binding of Isaac. She rescued Lot from the fire on the Five Cities, whose smoking land and pillar of salt still stand as witnesses.

She led Jacob, fleeing his brother, showed him God's kingdom, made him rich and gave him the prize in his wrestling. She went down with Joseph into the pit and brought him a kingdom's scepters. She entered the soul of Moses, faced Pharaoh with signs, paid the slaves their wages, was their cloud and fire, brought them through the Red Sea and drowned their enemies. The righteous sang, and Wisdom opened the mouths of the mute and of babies.
readings: Read as retold history

Each hero is 'a righteous man' saved by Wisdom, each villain one who left her. The chapter adds details Genesis does not have (Adam rescued, Cain perished, the Flood because of him, the infants' song) that come from Jewish retellings of the stories.
Read as a pattern

With no names given, the stories become types: the righteous suffer, are guarded and are raised; the wicked destroy themselves. The pattern prepares for chapters 11–19, where Egypt and Israel are set side by side in seven contrasts.

views.C: Catholic readers see Wisdom's work in the patriarchs as God's saving plan running through history toward Christ, and the chapter as a model of reading the Old Testament through its types.
views.P: Protestants compare the chapter with Hebrews 11, where faith, not Wisdom, is the thread through the same heroes, and note where the chapter goes beyond Genesis.
views.H: Scholars read the chapter as an early example of Jewish 'rewritten Bible' and of the example list, a form known from Greek rhetoric and from Sirach 44–50 and Hebrews 11. Some suggest the heroes are left unnamed so that the pattern, not the name, carries the lesson.
views.J: Some details have later Jewish parallels: Josephus tells of the Egyptians' weapons washed ashore for Israel (Antiquities 2.349), and a teaching in the Talmud says infants sang at the sea (Bavli Sotah 30b). Whether Wisdom knew these traditions, or the later sources grew from it or from a tradition both share, cannot be shown.

echoes: Genesis 2–4; Genesis 6–9; Genesis 11–12; Genesis 19; Genesis 22; Genesis 27–33; Genesis 37–41; Exodus 3–15; Hebrews 11:1–31; Sirach 44–50; Acts 7:2–36

settings.what: Wisdom in history, from Adam to the Exodus
settings.by: The book's speaker, turning in 10:20 to address the Lord
settings.to: The readers, and at 10:20 God himself
settings.when: after the prayer for wisdom (9:18 'saved by wisdom')
settings.why: To prove the prayer's last line: Wisdom has always saved those who served her and ruined those who left her. For Jews living in Egypt, the climax was their own founding story: Israel rescued from the very land in which they now lived.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt (see the book's front page for the place and for the dates proposed, from the reign of Ptolemy IV, 221–204 BC, to AD 41–44). The story told here ends with Israel leaving Egypt, the land where these readers lived.
